summary: The heavens tell God’s glory day after day without words, and their message goes out to the ends of the earth.

context.title: The heavens are telling
paragraphs: This reading follows the Hebrew numbering, in which the psalm’s title counts as verse 1, so verses 2-5 here are verses 1-4 in many English Bibles. [c1] Psalm 19 moves from God’s glory in the heavens to praise of the Torah. [c2] The divine name changes with it, from El in verse 2 to the LORD when the law is praised. [c3]

Each day and each night hands the message on to the next in an unbroken tradition. [c4] Yet verse 4 says there is no speech and no words. [c5] The older English sense, that no language exists where their voice is unheard, is now widely given up: the heavens speak with a silent eloquence that still reaches the whole world. [c6]

Paul quotes verse 5 in Romans 10:18 in its Greek form, where the sound going out to all the earth becomes the voice of the gospel’s preachers. [c7] The Cambridge Bible sees in this a comparison: the gospel is proclaimed as widely as nature proclaims God’s glory. [c8] In the psalm itself the voice is the wordless witness of the sky. [c9]

translationNotes.summary: A participle: the heavens “are recounting” God’s glory, an ongoing act rather than a single declaration.
translationNotes.body: In the Piel the verb sāpar means to recount, rehearse or declare, and BDB lists this verse among its uses for rehearsing the praise of God. [c10] The form is a participle, and Keil and Delitzsch find in it the idea of perpetuity: the telling never stops. [c11] For this reason Ellicott prefers the English “the heavens are telling” to a simple present tense. [c12]

translationNotes.summary: Rāqîaʿ is “the expanse”, the vault of heaven pictured as something beaten out and spread over the earth.
translationNotes.body: BDB defines rāqîaʿ as an extended surface or expanse, as if beaten out, and lists this verse under the vault of heaven. [c13] The same word names the expanse made on the second day in Gen 1:6. [c14] The English “firmament” comes through the Greek stereōma of the Septuagint, which reflects the idea of the sky as a solid vault. [c15]

translationNotes.summary: The verb pictures a spring bubbling over: each day pours speech to the next as a fountain pours water.
translationNotes.body: The root nāḇaʿ means to flow, spring or bubble up, and in the causative form to pour forth, often of speech. [c16] Proverbs 18:4 uses the same root for a flowing stream, an image of wisdom. [c17] Keil and Delitzsch hear in the word the rich fullness of an inexhaustible spring, as the testimony passes on from one day to the next. [c18]

translationNotes.summary: Hebrew has “their line”, a measuring line; the ancient versions read “their sound”, as Paul quotes it.
translationNotes.body: The noun qav usually means a measuring line, and the Cambridge Bible keeps that sense here: the line marks the whole earth as the domain of the heavens’ message. [c19] The Greek and Latin versions read “their sound”, and BDB suggests the text should probably be read qōlām, “their sound”. [c20] Paul’s quotation in Rom 10:18 follows the Greek sound, phthongos. [c21]

claims.text: In the Hebrew text the superscription of Psalm 19 is verse 1, so Hebrew verses 19:2-5 correspond to English 19:1-4.
Psalm 19 turns from the revelation of God in nature (Hebrew verses 2-7) to the law of the Lord (from Hebrew verse 8).
Verse 2 names God as El, and when the psalm turns to the law the name Jehovah (YHWH) takes the place of God.
Each day and each night hands on the message to its successor in an unbroken tradition.
Psalm 19:4 says that there is no speech and there are no words.
Many commentators reject the Authorised Version’s sense of the verse and read it as a silent eloquence that reaches the whole world, though Barnes defends the older sense.
Romans 10:18 quotes Psalm 19:5 in its Greek form, and there the sound is the voice of the preachers.
Paul’s use compares the universality of the proclamation of the Gospel with the universality of the proclamation of God’s glory in nature.
In the original psalm the voice is the unspoken testimony of the works of nature, especially the heavenly bodies.
The Piel of סָפַר means recount, rehearse, declare, and BDB lists Ps 19:2 among uses for rehearsing the praise of God.
Keil and Delitzsch find the idea of perpetuity in the participle.
Ellicott proposes “the heavens are telling” as the better rendering.
BDB defines רָקִיעַ as an extended surface, (solid) expanse, as if beaten out, and lists Ps 19:2 under the vault of heaven.
Genesis 1:6 uses רָקִיעַ for the expanse made amid the waters.
The English word firmament comes from the Septuagint’s στερέωμα, from the idea that the heavens are a solid concave.
נָבַע means flow, spring, bubble up, and in the Hiphil pour forth, figuratively usually of speech; Ps 19:3 has the Hiphil יַבִּיעַ.
Proverbs 18:4 uses the participle נֹבֵעַ of a flowing stream as a picture of the source of wisdom.
Keil and Delitzsch see in הִבִּיעַ the rich fullness of an inexhaustible spring, the testimony passing from one day to the next.
קַו usually means a measuring line, and the Cambridge Bible explains the verse by the measuring line that marks the limits of possession: the whole earth is the heavens’ sphere.
The Septuagint, Vulgate and other ancient versions render the word “sound”, and BDB suggests reading קֹלָם, “their sound”.
Romans 10:18 quotes the verse with φθόγγος, following the Septuagint.
